Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Vignette:
The rain on the I-95 overpass had turned the asphalt into a mirror. Julian remembered the exact moment the tires lost traction, how the steering wheel went slack in his hands, how the guardrail rushed toward them with terrifying precision. He remembered the shattering of the windshield in a slow, crystalline cascade, and the sickening collapse of his brother’s side of the car. The thirty seconds before that moment were gone, swallowed by a white fog, and the first few seconds after were just a roar of sirens and a stranger’s shouting. When the memory returned, it arrived as fragments: the smell of spilled coffee and ozone, the way his brother had turned to speak, the cold steel of the seatbelt cutting into his chest. Each time it surfaced, a wave of crushing guilt flooded his throat. He was behind the wheel. He had promised his wife, Claire, they would arrive on time for the gala. He told himself repeatedly that the rain was too heavy, but the guilt settled into his bones anyway. When it hit, the emotion became so vast he had to stop breathing, drop his hands to his sides, and sit in his leather office chair until his pulse slowed. Over the months that followed, Julian found himself bracing for the next impact. In his Midtown studio, surrounded by muslin toiles and half-finished runway samples, any sudden metallic clang made his shoulders hike to his ears and his breath catch. He learned to wear thick gloves when handling tools to dampen the vibration that felt too much like the steering wheel. The nights were precise. He lay in their Westchester bedroom, staring at the ceiling, waiting for sleep that refused to come. His mind would start racing through garment delivery schedules, then wholesale prices, until dawn bleached the windows. Fear and horror would arrive unbidden during fittings, often blooming into a sharp, hot shame that left him unable to look at a client’s face. He stopped sketching for the autumn line. Instead of planning the season, he kept his desk cleared of future dates. When Claire asked about booking a summer cottage, he said they would have to wait. He had come to believe that committing to tomorrow was a kind of betrayal. To keep the other days from collapsing, he learned to saturate his mind. He listened to classical music at full volume while cutting fabric. He memorized catalog numbers. He stayed late at the studio, re-measuring hemlines until his fingers cramped, keeping his mind occupied so the quiet would not let the past bleed through. The distance between him and Claire grew into a quiet geography of closed doors. She noticed how he flinched at her car pulling into the driveway, how he avoided traffic news, how he would abruptly leave a room when conversations turned toward their children’s college applications. His studio manager had quietly warned him about missing critical preview appointments, but Julian kept pushing the calendar forward, telling himself he just needed more time. He was certain that leaving the desk clear would keep the future at bay. He did not know what was causing the paralysis, only that the past felt more immediate than the present. What frightened him most was the sudden, unbidden certainty that the next sound would be the brakes failing again. What finally brought him to his therapist’s office last Tuesday was a fitting room mirror. He had been adjusting a mannequin’s collar when a delivery truck backfired outside. His chest seized, his vision tunneled, and he realized he could not move for a full minute. When the feeling passed, he sank to the floor, exhausted by the sheer effort of holding his own life together. He no longer wanted to suppress the days. He wanted to remember his brother without drowning, to sleep without bracing, to step back into the studio and sketch a future that did not feel like a promise he could not keep.
